biography.currentRole: Former Georgia State Senator, District 35 (Jan 2023–Sep 2025, resigned to run for governor); currently running for Governor of Georgia
priorRoles: Chair, Atlanta Public Schools Board of Education (2018–2021); at-large member (2013–2021)
Associate Attorney, McKenna Long & Aldridge, Atlanta (2010–2014)
Teach For America corps member / middle school social studies teacher, Houston TX (post-college)
biography.education: B.A., University of Miami; J.D., Emory University School of Law
biography.background: Born July 19, 1983 in Columbus, Georgia. Of Afro-Puerto Rican descent; first-generation college graduate; son of immigrants (father Fernando Esteves). Grew up partly in Orlando, FL. Attorney and businessman. Three family businesses. Public school parent.
biography.residency: Atlanta (parts of Cobb and Fulton County, Senate District 35)

statedPositions.quote: fight to lower the cost of insurance premiums by expanding Medicaid and getting more Georgians insured, lower the cost of prescription drugs, expand our rural hospitals and clinics, and secure much-needed resources for senior care across the state
statedPositions.notes: Explicit Medicaid expansion commitment. Georgia is one of the few remaining non-expansion states.

statedPositions.quote: running for governor to overturn Georgia's restrictive abortion ban once and for all and restore a woman's right to make her own healthcare decisions with her doctor and her family, not politicians
statedPositions.notes: Explicit and central campaign commitment. Endorsed by Shanette Williams, mother of Amber Thurman, who died after being denied an emergency fetal removal procedure under Georgia's heartbeat law.

statedPositions.quote: fully funding our public schools and modernizing our school funding formula, increasing pay for Georgia's teachers, and expanding early learning programs... stood up against voucher schemes that siphon resources away from our public schools
statedPositions.notes: Anti-voucher position consistent throughout legislative and board of education service.

statedPositions.quote: Expanding access to safe and affordable universal childcare to support working families and providers... would guarantee access for all 3- and 4-year-olds with a mixed delivery system through both public and private providers using Georgia Lottery reserves that totaled roughly $2.4 billion in the last fiscal year
statedPositions.notes: Specific funding mechanism identified (Georgia Lottery reserves). Mixed public-private delivery model.

statedPositions.topic: housing — anti-private equity / supply increase / renter protections
statedPositions.quote: increase the housing supply, strengthen renter protections and continue standing up to the out-of-state corporations that squeeze Georgia families out of the housing market
statedPositions.notes: Three distinct components: (1) ban/limit private equity home purchases, (2) increase supply, (3) renter protections.

statedPositions.quote: prioritize local small businesses, making it easier for Georgians to access capital and build wealth for generations to come
statedPositions.notes: General value statement on website; more specific $1B fund proposal elsewhere.

statedPositions.quote: advocate for renewable energy sources, expanding public transportation, and fight to address environmental concerns that exist across the state
statedPositions.notes: General values statement; not detailed with specific policies. Prior 2021 op-ed supported zero-emission electric school buses. No specific climate legislation found in Senate record.

keyBillsSponsored.description: Sponsored legislation to repeal Georgia HB 481 (2019), the so-called 'heartbeat' bill that outlaws most abortions after detection of fetal heartbeat
keyBillsSponsored.outcome: Did not pass — Republicans held Senate majority
keyBillsSponsored.notes: Highly symbolic; signal of firm pro-abortion-rights position even as minority party member

keyBillsSponsored.bill: SB 199 — Health Savings Accounts for State Employees
keyBillsSponsored.description: Made health savings accounts available as a pre-tax deduction for Georgia state employees, including teachers. Signed into law.
keyBillsSponsored.notes: Bipartisan bill; his first passed legislation. Market-adjacent approach to healthcare benefits.

keyBillsSponsored.description: Proposed legislation that would stop private equity firms from being allowed to purchase single-family homes in Georgia
keyBillsSponsored.outcome: Introduced; outcome unclear (likely died in Republican-controlled committee)
keyBillsSponsored.notes: Central to his housing platform; became a core 2026 campaign promise

keyBillsSponsored.description: Requires Parole Board to provide written explanation when keeping someone incarcerated beyond their tentative parole date. Co-sponsored.
keyBillsSponsored.outcome: Died in committee in 2025; returned for consideration in 2026 session (Esteves resigned before vote)
keyBillsSponsored.notes: Modest reform bill focused on transparency, not abolition or wholesale restructuring. Bipartisan framing.

positionConflicts.topic: school choice — HSA bill vs. anti-voucher stance
positionConflicts.conflict: Esteves authored SB 199 establishing health savings accounts for state employees (market-based benefit design) while simultaneously opposing education vouchers. His 2026 universal childcare plan also uses a mixed public-private delivery model. This suggests pragmatic market-mechanism acceptance rather than pure public-sector purism on economic policy.

evidenceSummary.notes: Short legislative record (2 years in state Senate, minority party) limits voting-record evidence. However, the 2026 campaign has been extensively covered and his platform is clearly articulated on healthcare, housing, education, and reproductive rights. Main gaps are in climate (depth), criminal justice (breadth), and immigration. His background in education governance and corporate law creates an interesting blend — anti-corporate on housing/private equity but used market mechanisms (HSAs, mixed childcare delivery) on other issues.
